In 2026, the national average cost to install[interlocking pavers](https://www.angi.com/articles/what-are-interlocking-pavers.htm) is **$3,400** . Most homeowners pay between **$1,500** and **$7,000** , with the total driven by material choice, project size, and design complexity. A smaller 60-square-foot area can be covered for as little as **$350** , making interlocking pavers an accessible option for a range of budgets.


## Interlocking Paver Installation Cost by Type


Not all interlocking pavers are created equal, and your material choice will shape both the look and the cost of your project. Costs vary by paver type, as the breakdown below shows:


Type of Paver Average Installation Cost Per Square Foot in 2026


Outdoor pavers $8–$25


Indoor pavers $20–$30


Customized pavers $20–$50

### Outdoor Pavers


The most popular outdoor interlocking paver materials are concrete, natural slate, and clay brick, and they typically cost **$8 to $25 per square foot** . Rubber pavers are a less common alternative at **$6 to $11 per square foot** , and their softer surface makes them a practical choice for households with elderly residents or young children.


### Indoor Pavers


Indoor interlocking pavers are a lesser-known option, but materials like marble can create a sleek, elegant finish for interior spaces at **$20 to $30 per square foot** . Because marble stains easily, it’s not suited for outdoor use, so this category is best reserved for protected interior applications.


### Customized Pavers


Customized interlocking pavers offer the most design freedom, with costs ranging from **$20** **to $50 per square foot,** depending on the material and the complexity of your choices. Options include a wide range of colors such as red, teal, and brown, as well as distinctive shapes like hexagons or zigzags. Some homeowners even have pavers engraved or cut to unique specifications for a truly one-of-a-kind result.

## Interlocking Paver Installation Cost by Style: How Do Material Choices Compare?


Yuriy Afonkin / Adobe Stock


Your choice of paver style directly affects what you will pay per square foot, so understanding how common materials compare helps you set a realistic budget. The table below shows how interlocking paver costs break down by style:


Paver Style Average Cost Per Square Foot in 2026


Concrete stone $8–$15


Natural slate or stone $15–$50


Concrete brick $8–$15


Clay brick $10–$20


### Concrete Stone


Concrete pavers are among the most widely used paver materials, and they cost **$8 to $15 per square foot** . Its popularity comes from a combination of durability, versatility, and an accessible price point that suits most budgets.


### Natural Slate/Stone


Natural slate and stone pavers cost **$15 to $50 per square foot** , reflecting the more refined aesthetic they bring to a project. Specialty paver companies can also source flagstone, marble, and other natural stone varieties if you want a material beyond the standard options.


### Concrete Brick


Concrete brick delivers the look of natural brick with the durability of concrete, and it costs **$8 to $15 per square foot** . It is a practical middle-ground choice for homeowners who want a classic aesthetic without paying a premium for natural clay.


### Clay Brick


Clay brick is made from natural materials including clay and limestone, and it costs **$10 to $20 per square foot** , a modest step up from concrete brick. That slight premium buys a distinct, traditional aesthetic that many homeowners prefer for outdoor living spaces.


## Additional Interlocking Paver Cost Factors: What Affects the Price?


Several variables beyond material choice can shift the total cost of your interlocking paver installation, and understanding them helps you build a more accurate budget. Costs depend on the specific factors described below.


### Labor


Interlocking paver installation is demanding work, and most homeowners are better served by hiring a[paver installer near you](https://www.angi.com/nearme/paver-installation/) rather than attempting it themselves. Professional labor runs **$50 to $80** **per hour** or **$4 to $11** **per square foot** , with rates varying by time of year, location, and the complexity of the install.


### Permits


Depending on your location and the scope of your project, you may need a permit before work begins, and a[construction permit costs](https://www.angi.com/articles/how-much-does-building-permit-cost.htm) between **$150 and $2,000** on average. Interlocking paver installations, whether indoors or outdoors, fall toward the lower end of that range.


### Location and Accessibility


Where you live affects both material costs and labor rates for interlocking paver installation. Urban and coastal areas with higher costs of living tend to push prices up, while rural areas with less contractor competition can also result in higher quotes. A hard-to-reach installation site on your property adds time to the job, which increases labor costs as well.


### Design Complexity


Design complexity is a meaningful driver of labor costs because professionals often price by project length, and intricate patterns take longer to complete. As Angi Expert Review Board member Matt DiBara of DiBara Masonry notes, straight-line layouts are always more affordable than curved ones, which require additional time for the special cutting involved.

## Why You Should Hire a Contractor for Interlocking Paver Installation


[Hiring a local contractor](https://www.angi.com/nearme/general-contractors/) costs more upfront, but you benefit from faster results, less risk of damage, and a professional finish. Pros bring specialized equipment and experience to a project, making the process smoother and often saving you money in the long run.


### Here’s why it’s ideal to hire a contractor


Hiring a local contractor to install interlocking pavers ensures a proper, long-lasting installation. Here are some of the top reasons to work with a pro:


-


Contractors know how to properly grade the site and compact the base, which is crucial for preventing water damage, shifting pavers, and long-term failure.


-


Pros have access to commercial-grade tools like plate compactors and levels that ensure a smoother, more durable finish than basic DIY kits.


-


A professional installation minimizes the risk of common mistakes like incorrect measurements or poor site preparation, which can be costly and time-consuming to correct mid-project.


-


Most local contractors offer warranties on their workmanship, protecting your investment against defects or future issues that a DIY project would not be covered for.


### If you want to DIY interlocking paver installation


If you want to take on some aspects of the project yourself, here are a few DIY tasks that can help save time and labor costs:


-


Remove objects, furniture, or debris from the installation site before the pros arrive to save on prep time.


-


Work with a designer to finalize your design and finish choices early on so you understand the entire scope of your project.


-


Have old flooring removed ahead of time to allow contractors to start with a blank slate.


-


Do any necessary paint touch ups on walls or baseboard yourself when the project is complete.


Next Steps: Finalize Your Project With a Contractor


-


Discuss paver patterns, colors, and materials to ensure they meet your aesthetic and functional needs.


-


Determine the required drainage for the area to prevent problems in the future.


-


Ask about the type of edge restraint they plan to use, including plastic on concrete, and why.


-


Inquire if they are able to check soil conditions, especially if you have clay soil which may require a deeper base.


-


Get a clear estimate for the total project including a best- and worst-case scenario timeline.

Frequently Asked Questions


When many homeowners think of pavers, they think of concrete stone pavers laid in sand. Clay brick is a close second in terms of the look most people want in their outdoor living spaces when they consider such a project. The good thing is that every material of paver is super durable and rated to last a long time.


Interlocking pavers offer a number of advantages over regular pavers. For instance, they’re more durable, more resistant to shifting, and easier to repair. There are also permeable options that allow for drainage. However, interlocking pavers are more often more expensive than regular pavers and are prone to growing weeds over time.


Interlocking pavers can last for 50 years or more if they are installed correctly and properly maintained. The foundation is the most critical factor for longevity; a poorly prepared base will significantly shorten the patio's life. Routine maintenance includes applying a sealant regularly, managing any weeds that grow between the pavers, and avoiding harsh de-icing chemicals or metal shovels in the winter, as they can damage the surface over time.
